design_detail: Double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized, within-person laboratory study at the General Clinical Research Center of Washington University School of Medicine in 15 healthy men. Each man had four infusion conditions on four separate mornings on non-consecutive days (mean 2.6 days apart, SD 1.1): saline and three fixed intravenous ketamine doses designed to hold three different steady plasma concentrations (targets 13.5, 45 and 150 ng/mL). Each condition began with a loading dose over 10 minutes followed immediately by a maintenance infusion lasting to 120 minutes. Clinical ratings and the cognitive battery began 30 minutes after the start, by which time the authors establish that plasma concentrations were steady, and ran during the maintenance infusion; blood for ketamine, norketamine, epinephrine, norepinephrine, insulin, glucose and cortisol, and cardiovascular monitoring, were taken at 0, 20, 60 and 120 minutes. Measures: BPRS (total, positive and negative subscales), Scale for the Assessment of Negative Symptoms (SANS), a clinician-administered Clinical and Adverse Events Checklist, and a cognitive battery given in fixed order with two counterbalanced sets of matched task versions: immediate and delayed paragraph recall, delayed match to sample (two subtasks), a modified Stroop task, a continuous performance task, verbal fluency and a spatial delayed response task. Abbreviated unblinded ratings were made before and after each infusion and about 48 hours later. Only men were studied, for the reasons the authors give (the pharmacokinetic data available for the dose calculations came almost entirely from men, and a lower threshold for NMDA-antagonist neurotoxicity had been reported in female rats).
can_establish: Whether, within the same men, three fixed intravenous ketamine infusions producing measured steady plasma concentrations change psychiatric symptom ratings and performance on a battery of cognitive tasks compared with saline, and how those changes order across the concentrations reached: the dose-response relation for positive and negative symptom ratings and for verbal and non-verbal declarative memory, measured during the infusion in 15 healthy men.
cannot_establish: Anything about women (none were studied), about repeated or non-medical use, about other routes, or about people with psychiatric histories (all were excluded, as was any previous use of ketamine or phencyclidine); anything beyond the 48-hour check, which used an abbreviated unblinded rating and no cognitive testing; and, because the non-memory tasks showed no effect, it cannot show that those functions are spared rather than that the tasks were less sensitive, a limitation the authors state.

sample.recruitment: Local advertisement; the protocol was approved by the Human Studies Committee at Washington University School of Medicine and all participants gave written informed consent (p. 107).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Inclusion: male, aged 18 to 40, able to give informed consent. Exclusion: any Axis I or Cluster A Axis II psychiatric disorder, including any substance use disorder in the previous 12 months, assessed with the Diagnostic Instrument for Genetic Studies and reviewed by a senior clinician, with the Family Instrument for Genetic Studies used to look for psychopathology in first-degree relatives (none was found); a long list of medical exclusions (diabetes, treated or untreated hypertension, glaucoma, dehydration, epilepsy, endocrine disorders, recent abdominal, limb or intrathoracic surgery, cardiac conditions causing haemodynamic compromise or conduction problems, respiratory conditions causing hypoxia, fever, body weight below 80% or above 120% of ideal, any condition known to interfere with cognitive performance); exclusion of narcotics, corticosteroids, spironolactone, benzodiazepines or other sedative-hypnotics and drugs affecting cardiac conduction; any past use of phencyclidine or ketamine; and mental retardation by DSM-IV criteria (pp. 107-108).
sample.demographics: 15 men; mean age 21.7 years (SD 3.2), education 14.7 years (SD 2.2), handedness decile score 6.3 (SD 2.7), body mass index 22.4 kg/m2 (SD 3.4). All used English as a first language; 10 white Americans, 3 black Americans, 1 Hispanic American and 1 Asian American (p. 108).
sample.attrition: No one withdrew. All but one participant on one treatment day completed almost all of the cognitive battery; several had missing or invalid data points on the computerized tasks for technical reasons (reaction-time data from the continuous performance task were filtered for outliers), and one participant with nausea at the high dose could not do all the cognitive assessments and missed a final blood sample (pp. 110, 113). The degrees of freedom of the analyses vary accordingly (for example F3,41 for paragraph recall, F3,40 for delayed match to sample, and post-hoc t tests on 13 or 14 degrees of freedom).
sample.selection_effects: Young, healthy, screened men with no previous exposure to ketamine or phencyclidine and no psychiatric or substance-use history: the sample with the least tolerance and the lowest psychiatric vulnerability, chosen deliberately. Both the symptom response and the memory response in this group may differ from those of women, of older people, and of people who have used ketamine or other drugs before. The authors state the restriction to men explicitly and give their reasons (pp. 107, 110).

exposure.measurement: Plasma ketamine and norketamine measured by gas chromatography at a commercial laboratory (National Medical Services, Philadelphia), with samples at 0, 20, 60 and 120 minutes placed on ice, centrifuged and stored at minus 80 degrees Celsius. Low-dose concentrations fell below the assay threshold. Plasma epinephrine and norepinephrine (single isotope derivative radioenzymatic method), glucose (glucose oxidase), insulin and cortisol (radioimmunoassay) were also measured, as potential confounders of the cognitive outcomes (p. 110).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only, as the investigators gave them, calculated from published pharmacokinetic parameters to hold steady plasma concentrations of 150, 45 and 13.5 ng/mL: loading doses of 0.27, 0.081 and 0.0243 mg/kg given intravenously over 10 minutes, each followed immediately by a maintenance infusion of 0.00225, 0.000675 or 0.0002025 mg/kg per minute to 120 minutes, and a saline condition; the highest total dose was 0.54 mg/kg over the session. The four conditions were given in randomized order on four separate mornings, on non-consecutive days a mean of 2.6 days apart (SD 1.1), after a fast of at least 8 hours (pp. 108-110). The high-dose condition was designed to reproduce the plasma concentrations at the time points at which symptoms had been measured in the 1994 study of Krystal et al.
exposure.polysubstance: Substance use disorders in the previous 12 months were excluded by structured interview and any past use of phencyclidine or ketamine was an exclusion criterion; no urine drug screen, no quantification of alcohol, tobacco or caffeine use and no abstinence requirement other than the overnight fast are described (pp. 107-108).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: A fast of at least 8 hours before each study morning, imposed to keep glucose from confounding the cognitive measures; no drug or alcohol abstinence period and no biological verification are described (p. 108).

comparison.controls: Each man's own saline condition, one of the four randomized infusion days (within-person placebo), with the two active low conditions also serving as internal comparisons for the dose-response analysis.
comparison.matching: Within-person comparison across four days; two different sets of the task battery, offering the matched task versions in two different orders across study days, were counterbalanced across participants (p. 109). The order of the four infusion conditions was randomized; sequence generation and concealment are not described.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a within-person comparison; each day's pre-infusion assessment is that day's reference, and the primary symptom analyses model baseline, infusion and post-infusion time points.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable (the same men served as their own controls).

outcomes.instruments: Clinical, rated blind to condition during the infusion: the 18-item Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (BPRS) with its classic subfactors, the positive subscale being hallucinatory behavior, conceptual disorganization and unusual thought content and the negative subscale blunted affect, emotional withdrawal and motor retardation; the 25-item Scale for the Assessment of Negative Symptoms (SANS), with subscales for affective flattening, alogia, avolition-apathy, anhedonia-asociality and attention; and a clinician-administered Clinical and Adverse Events Checklist, a five-point Likert scale of items taken from the anaesthesiology literature. For the BPRS hallucinatory behavior item the authors used the original item description so that perceptual distortions as well as hallucinations could be scored, which widens that item. Abbreviated unblinded BPRS and checklist ratings were made before and after each infusion and about 48 hours later. Cognitive: immediate and delayed (30-minute) verbatim recall of two recorded narratives of 44 pieces of information each, scored for correct recall and commission errors (verbal declarative memory, the Wechsler paragraph recall test, with eight paragraphs shown to be comparable); a computerized delayed match to sample task in two subtasks, 'a' with 20 line drawings and a 3.5-minute filled delay and 'b' with 40 drawings, each followed by 10 three-choice recognition trials (non-verbal declarative memory); a multiple-version modification of the Stroop colour-word interference task (selective attention); a computerized continuous performance task with letters (sustained attention); word list generation (verbal fluency, as a measure of prefrontal function); and a spatial delayed response task with 5-second and 120-second delays and cue-present trials, scored as mean distance from the target (spatial working memory at short delays and spatial working or declarative memory at long delays) (pp. 108-109).
outcomes.validity_norms: The paragraph recall test is cited as validated and sensitive, and the Stroop, continuous performance, verbal fluency and spatial delayed response tasks are standard; the eight paragraphs are stated to be comparable in recall and sensitivity on unpublished data, and the delayed match to sample task is adapted from animal and human lesion work. No norms are applied to any score, and the SANS and BPRS are used in healthy people, where almost all items sit at the floor on placebo (SANS subscale means of 0.0 to 0.9 on placebo, Table 1).
outcomes.operationalization: 'Impairment' is a significant effect of treatment condition on a task score across the four steady-state conditions, followed by paired t tests between dose levels; 'positive' and 'negative symptoms' are the BPRS subscale sums and the SANS total. All measures are acute and were taken during the maintenance infusion, that is during steady-state concentrations; the only later assessment is an abbreviated unblinded rating about 48 hours afterwards, with no cognitive testing. The study is in healthy men only; nothing in it concerns patients or lasting effects.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Partial and explicitly reasoned. The authors treat the primary hypotheses (positive symptoms, negative symptoms, verbal and non-verbal memory) as a limited number of planned tests not requiring adjustment, and give Bonferroni-adjusted critical p values alongside unadjusted ones for the exploratory analyses: critical p=0.01 for the five SANS subscales, 0.0125 for the other BPRS subscales, 0.01 for the plasma variables, and 0.025, 0.025 and 0.017 for the three primary measures when adjusted (pp. 110, 112, 114). Editors' count of the outcome measures analysed: BPRS total, positive and negative subscales, SANS total and 5 subscales, paragraph recall, delayed match to sample, Stroop, continuous performance, verbal fluency and spatial delayed response, plus 6 plasma measures. Post-hoc paired t tests between dose levels are uncorrected.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: The full clinical assessments and the cognitive battery during the infusion were performed blind to treatment assignment (p. 108), which is stated more specifically than in most ketamine studies; the pre- and post-infusion and 48-hour ratings were unblinded. No blinding check is reported, and the high-dose condition produced nausea in 6 of 15 participants and the moderate condition in 1, with 2 participants vomiting (the paper does not say in which condition), and dose-dependent reports of dizziness, a dream-like state and altered sense of time, so blinding is unlikely to have held at the higher concentrations.

analysis.effect_sizes: F statistics, paired t tests and plotted means with SE; no confidence intervals and no standardized effect sizes. Symptoms: BPRS positive subscale main effect of treatment condition F3,42=21.84 (p<0.0001); BPRS negative subscale F3,42=2.89 (p=0.047); SANS total F3,42=10.55 (p<0.0001); BPRS total across baseline, infusion and washout, treatment condition by time F6,83=17.62 (p=0.0001), and during the steady state F3,42=21.60 (p=0.0001). Memory: total (immediate plus delayed) paragraph recall F3,41=5.11 (p=0.004), immediate F3,41=3.92 (p=0.02), delayed F3,41=5.03 (p=0.005), with a main effect of recall condition F1,14=46.14 (p=0.0001) and no interaction of treatment with recall condition; delayed match to sample F3,40=2.93 (p=0.045). The only magnitude the paper states in natural units is the fall in total paragraph recall from placebo to the high dose, 21.2 bits, which it calls an 18.6% decrease. Editors' calculation of within-person standardized differences from the printed post-hoc t values: placebo against high dose about 0.88 for paragraph recall (t13=3.30) and about 0.64 for the moderate-dose comparison (t14=2.47); these are approximate because the paired t values come from analyses with different numbers of complete cases.
analysis.covariates: Drowsiness, taken from the adverse-events checklist, was used as a covariate in the models for verbal and non-verbal memory: no main effect of drowsiness and no interaction with treatment condition (p. 113). Plasma epinephrine, norepinephrine, glucose and cortisol, all of which changed with condition, were covaried in the same models from the time points closest to the cognitive measures, again with no main effect or interaction (pp. 113-114). No adjustment for order or period; sex is not applicable.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned, but the primary hypotheses (dose-dependent increases in positive and negative symptoms and dose-dependent decreases in hippocampally associated memory performance) are stated in the introduction before the results and carried through the analysis plan, with exploratory analyses labelled as such (pp. 107, 110).
analysis.selective_reporting: Low concern by the standards of this literature: the analysis section states in advance which tests are primary and which exploratory, gives Bonferroni-adjusted critical values for the exploratory ones, and reports the null results in full (no effect on the Stroop task, the continuous performance task, verbal fluency or the spatial delayed response task, and a non-significant SANS alogia and attention subscale). Against this, the cognitive results appear only as plotted means with SE in Figures 4 and 5, with no table of means; the delayed match to sample effect is reported as significant in the univariate analysis while not significant in the multivariate one; and the qualitative subject quotations are selected to illustrate the symptoms.
analysis.power: Not reported; no sample-size calculation. The primary symptom and verbal memory effects are large and ordered across concentrations. The weaker results rest on little: the delayed match to sample effect has F3,40=2.93, p=0.045 with post-hoc tests on 5 and 7 degrees of freedom, so it is based on as few as 6 to 8 complete pairs, which is why the authors call it preliminary; and the null results on the Stroop, continuous performance, verbal fluency and spatial delayed response tasks come from the same 15 men and cannot show that those functions are unaffected.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 15 healthy young men with no previous exposure to ketamine, intravenous infusions holding measured steady plasma concentrations of about 16 to 18 ng/mL (moderate) and about 87 to 88 ng/mL (high), read from Figure 6, whose values are not printed produced, during the infusion, a dose-ordered rise in BPRS positive symptom ratings and in SANS total scores, a smaller rise in BPRS negative symptom ratings, and a dose-ordered fall in verbal declarative memory (total paragraph recall fell by 21.2 bits, or 18.6%, from placebo to the high dose), with a weaker and less certain fall in non-verbal recognition memory. Immediate and delayed recall were affected similarly. No effect was detected on the Stroop task, the continuous performance task, verbal fluency or the spatial delayed response task. The memory effects survived adjustment for drowsiness, cortisol, glucose and the catecholamines. The syndrome was described as mild, and no abnormal symptoms were detected at the abbreviated 48-hour assessment.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says that the memory effect occurred 'at or below plasma concentrations producing other symptoms' and that increasing NMDA receptor hypofunction is associated with early occurring memory impairments followed by other schizophrenia-like symptoms (p. 106). The ordering rests on the figures' post-hoc comparisons: total paragraph recall was lower than placebo already at the low dose (t14=2.02, printed as p=0.03, one-tailed; p=0.06 two-tailed, editors' calculation), whereas the lowest condition at which a symptom measure differed from placebo was the moderate dose for BPRS positive symptoms, and the SANS total is compared with placebo only at the high dose. The low-dose plasma concentration was below the assay threshold and so was never measured, so the claim that memory is affected at a lower concentration than symptoms rests on one marginal one-tailed comparison at an unmeasured concentration. The 'preliminary evidence' wording for non-verbal memory is appropriate and is kept in the abstract. The discussion is careful about the null results, stating that differences in task sensitivity could contribute to the apparent selectivity (p. 115), and about the restriction to men. The claim that such doses “can be used safely in healthy young males” in closely monitored experimental settings (p. 114) rests on 15 men followed up by an abbreviated unblinded rating at 48 hours. Framing the findings as a model of memory impairment and psychosis in schizophrenia, in the title and throughout, extends a healthy-volunteer drug study to a disorder none of the participants had.

timeline.event: A randomized saline-controlled study of 40-minute infusions in 18 healthy volunteers reported the acute rise in BPRS positive and negative symptom scores and a fall in delayed word recall, with predicted rather than measured plasma concentrations; this study's high-dose condition was designed to reproduce those predicted concentrations

A placebo-controlled 1-hour infusion study in 15 healthy volunteers reported lower free recall and recognition memory and raised BPRS thought-disorder and withdrawal-retardation scores, and argued that the memory effect was not secondary to attention
Positron emission tomography studies of (S)- and (R)-ketamine in healthy volunteers, to be appraised from their full texts, relate the psychopathological profile to regional brain metabolism
An infusion study in people with schizophrenia reported a brief return of their own symptoms, which this paper's model implies (to be appraised from the full text)

replication.where_it_stands: The acute, dose-ordered rise in psychotic-like symptom ratings and fall in verbal declarative memory during subanaesthetic ketamine infusions in healthy volunteers is consistent across this study and the earlier work it set out to extend, and this is the study that ties those effects to measured steady plasma concentrations rather than predicted ones. What differs between laboratories is the pattern across non-memory tasks: effects on vigilance, verbal fluency and card sorting were reported at 0.5 mg/kg over 40 minutes (Krystal et al., 1994) but not at these steady concentrations, which the authors attribute to the dose and the steady-state conditions and, in part, to differences in task sensitivity. Whether memory is affected at lower concentrations than the symptoms is still untested, because the lowest condition here fell below the assay threshold.

funding.funder: As printed (p. 115): supported by an Independent Scientist Award (MH01510; JWN) from the National Institute of Mental Health, MH53363 (JWN), a Scientist Development Award from the National Institute of Drug Abuse (DA00290; NBF), an Established Investigator Award from NARSAD (JWO), a Research Scientist Award from the NIMH (MH38894; JWO), AG11355 (JWO) and U.S.P.H.S. 5M01 RR00036 and P60-DK20579.
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: the paper carries no conflict-of-interest statement, which was not usual practice in 1999.
funding.affiliations_note: Academic departments of psychiatry, anesthesiology and pathology at Washington University in St Louis, with co-authors at the University of Washington and the Seattle Veterans Affairs Medical Center; the work was carried out in a General Clinical Research Center. The last author's laboratory had reported the rodent neurotoxicity findings that the paper's safety reasoning relies on, and an unpublished finding of theirs (that norketamine is 7 to 10 times less potent than ketamine at the NMDA receptor) is used to dismiss norketamine's contribution. No industry sponsor is named.

what_would_settle_it: A study of the same design with concentrations low enough to be measured at the bottom of the range and dense enough to estimate separate concentration-response curves for memory and for symptom ratings, with tasks matched for difficulty and reliability so that selectivity can be distinguished from sensitivity, in women as well as men and in people with previous ketamine exposure, with blinding tested and with cognitive testing repeated days and weeks afterwards rather than an abbreviated symptom rating at 48 hours.

domains.domain: Randomization process (order of the four infusion conditions)
domains.note: The four conditions were given in randomized order and the two sets of task versions were counterbalanced across participants, but no sequence generation or allocation concealment is described and no period or order effect is reported. The symptom analyses include each day's own baseline, and Figure 1 shows the four baselines close together (about 19.2 to 19.5 BPRS points).

Conditions were given on non-consecutive days a mean of 2.6 days apart (SD 1.1), which is far more than enough for elimination; plasma norketamine was 0.0 at the start of each condition (Table 2). Practice effects are addressed by matched task versions in two counterbalanced orders, and the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test, which cannot be repeated, was not used.

The infusion days are described as double-blind and the clinical and cognitive assessments during the infusion were made blind to condition, which is better documented than in most studies of this kind; but no blinding check is reported, and the higher conditions produced nausea in 6 of 15 participants, vomiting in 2, and dose-dependent dizziness, a dream-like state and altered sense of time, so participants and raters are unlikely to have remained blind at the high concentration. The pre-infusion, post-infusion and 48-hour ratings were explicitly unblinded.

No one withdrew, but the computerized tasks lost data for technical reasons and one participant could not complete the battery because of nausea at the high dose, which is a drug effect and therefore not missing at random. The resulting numbers are not stated; they have to be inferred from degrees of freedom (F3,41, F3,40, t on 13 or 5 or 7 degrees of freedom). The multivariate analysis of the delayed match to sample task, which requires complete data, was not significant while the univariate one was.

Plasma assays and the computerized tasks are objective; the paragraph recall scoring is a modification of established methods and the raters were blind during the infusion, which lowers the concern. The symptom instruments are clinician ratings in a probably recognizable condition, and the BPRS hallucinatory behavior item was deliberately widened to score perceptual distortions as well as hallucinations, which raises the positive subscale relative to its usual meaning.

The hypotheses are stated before the results, the primary and exploratory tests are separated, Bonferroni-adjusted critical values are given for the exploratory analyses with the unadjusted values alongside, and all the null results are reported. The absence of a table of cognitive means is a presentational weakness, not selective reporting.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: This is the strongest design among the early ketamine laboratory studies: four randomized within-person conditions with measured steady plasma concentrations, assessments made blind to condition, pre-specified primary hypotheses, correction for the exploratory tests, and covariate checks for drowsiness, cortisol, glucose and the catecholamines, all of which leave the dose-ordered symptom and verbal memory findings internally strong. The overall judgment is set by blinding: no blinding check is reported and the high condition produced nausea, vomiting and marked subjective effects in a study whose symptom outcomes are clinician ratings. The source can be cited for the concentration-response relation between measured steady plasma ketamine (about 16 to 18 and about 87 to 88 ng/mL, read from Figure 6) and BPRS positive, BPRS negative and SANS ratings and verbal declarative memory in 15 healthy young men during a 2-hour infusion, for the measured plasma ketamine, norketamine, cortisol, glucose and catecholamine values, and for the absence of a detectable effect on the Stroop, continuous performance, verbal fluency and spatial delayed response tasks at those concentrations. It cannot be cited for women, for people with previous ketamine exposure or psychiatric illness, for any effect beyond 48 hours, for the claim that memory is affected at lower concentrations than symptoms, or for the safety of ketamine administration.

key_findings.finding: BPRS positive symptom ratings (hallucinatory behavior, conceptual disorganization, unusual thought content) rose with the infusion condition in 15 healthy men: main effect of treatment condition F3,42=21.84 (p<0.0001), with paired comparisons t14=5.07 (p=0.0001), t14=4.99 (p=0.0001) and t14=2.17 (p=0.02).
key_findings.locator: Results > Behavioral Results > Positive Symptoms, 1st paragraph; Figure 2 and its legend
key_findings.note: Editors' reading of Figure 2, whose values are not printed: the three-item subscale has a floor of 3; the placebo and low-dose bars sit at that floor, the moderate-dose mean is about 3.5 and the high-dose mean about 5.1, so the largest change is about 2.1 points on a subscale running from 3 to 21. The printed p values correspond to one-tailed paired tests (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: BPRS negative symptom ratings (blunted affect, emotional withdrawal, motor retardation) also changed with condition, more weakly: F3,42=2.89 (p=0.047), with increases between placebo and high dose (t14=-1.95, p=0.04), between low and moderate doses (t14=-2.26, p=0.02) and between low and high doses (t14=-2.32, p=0.02).
key_findings.locator: Results > Behavioral Results > Negative Symptoms, only paragraph
key_findings.note: This result would not survive the Bonferroni critical value of 0.025 that the authors apply to the primary measures in the Discussion (p. 114), and the Discussion's list of robustly significant findings substitutes the SANS total for this subscale. The printed post-hoc p values are one-tailed; two-tailed, the placebo against high dose comparison gives p=0.07 (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Scale for the Assessment of Negative Symptoms (SANS) total scores rose with condition: F3,42=10.55 (p<0.0001), with paired comparisons t14=4.44 (p=0.0003), t14=4.18 (p=0.0005), t14=2.54 (p=0.01) and t14=1.61 (p=0.07). By subscale (Table 1, means and SD across the four conditions placebo, low, moderate, high): affective flattening 0.2 (0.6), 0.0 (0.0), 0.7 (1.1), 1.4 (2.1), F3,42=4.49, p=0.008; alogia 0.0 (0.0), 0.1 (0.3), 0.3 (0.6), 0.6 (1.1), F3,42=2.51, p=0.07; avolition-apathy 0.2 (0.6), 0.2 (0.6), 0.5 (0.9), 1.5 (1.5), F3,42=9.08, p=0.0001; anhedonia-asociality 0.3 (0.9), 0.2 (0.6), 0.8 (2.0), 2.9 (3.2), F3,42=6.51, p=0.001; attention 0.9 (1.1), 0.9 (1.2), 0.5 (0.7), 1.3 (1.3), F3,42=2.61, p=0.06.
key_findings.locator: Results > Behavioral Results > Negative Symptoms (p. 111); Figure 3 and its legend (p. 111); Table 1 (p. 112)
key_findings.note: Editors' reading of Figure 3, whose values are not printed: SANS totals of about 1.6 on placebo, 1.4 at the low dose, 2.9 at the moderate dose and 7.7 at the high dose, on a 25-item scale. The subscale standard deviations are as large as the means or larger, so the subscale differences rest on a few participants; the attention subscale is not ordered by dose.

key_findings.finding: BPRS total scores rose during the infusion and returned afterwards: treatment condition by time interaction across baseline, infusion and washout F6,83=17.62 (p=0.0001); during the steady-state conditions the effect of treatment condition was F3,42=21.60 (p=0.0001). Positive symptom subscale scores accounted for the largest part of the change (treatment condition by time F6,83=22.54, p=0.0001), with a smaller effect for the negative symptom subscale (F6,83=2.73, p=0.02).
key_findings.locator: Results > Behavioral Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 1 and its legend
key_findings.note: Editors' reading of Figure 1, whose values are not printed: the four baselines lie between about 19.2 and 19.5 on the 18-item BPRS (floor 18); at the infusion time point the high-dose mean is about 23.3 and the moderate about 20.2, while the low-dose and placebo means stay near 19.2; at washout all four fall to about 18.6 to 19.1, that is to or below their own baselines. The baseline and post-washout ratings in Figure 1 are the abbreviated unblinded ones (p. 108), so the condition by time interaction mixes blinded infusion ratings with unblinded ones and the return to baseline 60 minutes after the infusion is an unblinded observation.

key_findings.finding: Verbal declarative memory fell with the infusion condition: total (immediate plus delayed) paragraph recall F3,41=5.11 (p=0.004), immediate recall F3,41=3.92 (p=0.02) and delayed recall F3,41=5.03 (p=0.005), with a main effect of recall condition (immediate against delayed) F1,14=46.14 (p=0.0001) and no interaction between treatment condition and recall condition. The mean fall in total correct recall from placebo to the high dose was 21.2 bits, which the paper reports as an 18.6% decrease.
key_findings.locator: Results > Cognitive Results > Paragraph Recall, only paragraph; Figure 4 and its legend
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: 21.2 bits as 18.6% implies about 114 bits recalled on placebo, which matches the plotted placebo mean; the two narratives together contain 88 pieces of information, scored over immediate and delayed recall, so the units are the paper's own scoring of bits recalled. Editors' reading of Figure 4, whose values are not printed: about 114 bits on placebo, about 103 at the low and moderate doses and about 93 at the high dose. Post-hoc paired comparisons in the legend: t13=3.30 (p=0.003), t14=2.47 (p=0.01), t14=2.02 (p=0.03), t13=1.70 (p=0.06) and t13=1.57 (p=0.07), all one-tailed.

key_findings.finding: Non-verbal declarative memory (delayed match to sample, subtasks a and b combined) also changed with condition: F3,40=2.93 (p=0.045), with paired comparisons t5=2.04 (p=0.05) and t7=2.78 (p=0.01). The effect appeared in the univariate analysis but not in the multivariate analysis, which requires complete data for each participant and so included fewer people; there was again no interaction with the recall condition.
key_findings.locator: Results > Cognitive Results > DMS (p. 112, foot of the left column to the top of the right column); Figure 5 and its legend (p. 113)
key_findings.note: The degrees of freedom of the post-hoc tests (5 and 7) imply as few as 6 to 8 complete pairs, so this is the weakest of the cognitive findings; the authors describe it in the abstract as preliminary evidence. Editors' reading of Figure 5, whose values are not printed: a mean ratio of correct to total responses of about 1.34 on placebo, 1.43 at the low dose, 1.32 at the moderate dose and 1.15 at the high dose, that is not ordered by dose across the lower three conditions.

key_findings.finding: Comparisons with placebo across the four conditions, as the figures mark them: total paragraph recall was lower than placebo at the low dose (t14=2.02, p=0.03), the moderate dose (t14=2.47, p=0.01) and the high dose (t13=3.30, p=0.003); BPRS positive symptom ratings were marked as different from placebo only at the moderate dose (t14=2.17, p=0.02) and above; and the SANS total is compared with placebo only at the high dose (t14=4.44, p=0.0003). The low-dose plasma concentration was below the assay threshold.
key_findings.locator: Figure 2 and its legend (p. 111); Figure 3 and its legend (p. 111); Figure 4 and its legend (p. 112); Figure 6 (p. 113)
key_findings.note: This set of comparisons is the whole of the evidence for the abstract's statement that the memory effect occurs at or below the concentrations producing other symptoms. All the printed p values are one-tailed; two-tailed, the low-dose recall comparison gives p=0.06 and the moderate-dose BPRS comparison p=0.048 (editors' calculation). Editors' reading of the figures: the brackets run placebo to low, placebo to moderate and placebo to high in Figure 4, placebo to moderate, low to moderate and moderate to high in Figure 2, and placebo to high, low to high, moderate to high and low to moderate in Figure 3.

key_findings.finding: No significant effect of treatment condition was detected, with adjusted or unadjusted p values, on the modified Stroop task, the continuous performance task, the verbal fluency task or the spatial delayed response task, including its 120-second delay condition.
key_findings.locator: Results > Cognitive Results > Other Cognitive Tasks, only paragraph (p. 112); Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 115), for the 120-second delay condition
key_findings.note: No statistics at all are printed for these four tasks, so the size of the non-effects cannot be judged; the authors state in the Discussion that differences in the sensitivity or difficulty of the tasks could contribute to the apparent selectivity (p. 115).

key_findings.finding: Plasma ketamine was sampled at 0, 20, 60 and 120 minutes; it peaked at the 20-minute sample and was stable at 60 and 120 minutes in the moderate and high conditions, while the low-condition concentrations stayed below the assay threshold. Steady state by 30 minutes is the authors' calculation from the 20- and 60-minute levels and the half-lives, not a measurement. The condition by time interaction was F9,125=73.62 (p=0.0001).
key_findings.locator: Results > Plasma Results, 1st paragraph; Figure 6 and its legend
key_findings.note: Editors' reading of Figure 6, whose values are not printed: in the high-dose condition about 110 ng/mL at 20 minutes falling to about 88 at 60 minutes and about 87 at 120; in the moderate condition about 27, 18 and 16 ng/mL; the assay threshold line sits at about 10 ng/mL. The target steady concentrations were 150, 45 and 13.5 ng/mL (p. 109), so the measured steady concentrations were roughly three-fifths and two-fifths of target (editors' calculation); the paper does not comment on this difference.

key_findings.finding: Plasma norketamine did not reach a steady state but rose throughout the infusion: in the moderate condition 0.0 (SD 0.0) at 0 minutes, 16.9 (8.8) at 20, 20.9 (3.9) at 60 and 23.3 (4.2) ng/mL at 120; in the high condition 0.0 (0.0), 37.5 (19.2), 64.3 (11.9) and 79.5 (19.0) ng/mL; condition by sample time F9,125=85.69 (p=0.0001).
key_findings.note: At 120 minutes in the high condition plasma norketamine (79.5 ng/mL) was close to the measured ketamine concentration. The authors dismiss a contribution from norketamine on the basis of their own unpublished data that it is 7 to 10 times less potent than ketamine at the NMDA receptor (p. 113).

key_findings.finding: Plasma cortisol, glucose, epinephrine and norepinephrine changed with condition (condition by sample time: cortisol F9,125=8.84, p=0.0001; glucose F9,125=3.10, p=0.002; norepinephrine F9,125=10.50, p=0.0001; epinephrine F9,125=2.38, p=0.02, against a Bonferroni critical p of 0.01), while insulin did not. In the high condition cortisol rose from 13.7 (SD 5.4) micrograms/dL at 0 minutes to 18.3 (5.6), 21.4 (10.0) and 22.1 (12.4) at 20, 60 and 120 minutes, against a fall on placebo from 16.7 (6.9) to 10.5 (4.4); norepinephrine rose from 145.1 (58.0) to 308.3 (155.1) pg/mL at 20 minutes and returned to 167.6 (63.2) by 120 minutes. Covarying these variables, and drowsiness, left the verbal and non-verbal memory effects of treatment condition unchanged.
key_findings.locator: Results > Plasma Results, 2nd paragraph (p. 113); Table 2 (p. 114); Results > Additional Clinical and Adverse Events, and Safety Measures, 2nd paragraph (p. 113)
key_findings.note: The epinephrine change at 20 minutes in the high condition has a standard deviation larger than the mean (170.1, SD 308.2 pg/mL), so it rests on a few large values.

key_findings.finding: Adverse effects and tolerability: ketamine transiently raised diastolic and systolic blood pressure and produced very short-lived increases in pulse rate that had resolved by the 20-minute time point, with no fall in blood oxygen saturation. Six of the 15 men had nausea during the high-dose condition and one at the moderate dose, with 2 vomiting; one man with nausea at the high dose could not complete all the cognitive assessments and missed a final blood sample. During the loading dose, drowsiness, difficulty concentrating, dizziness, confusion, lightheadedness, a feeling of being high, exhilaration, floating sensations, paraesthesias, a dream-like state and a changed sense of time all rose with dose, all at moderate levels or below; during the steady state the same symptoms stayed at mild levels or below. No abnormal symptoms were detected at the assessment about 48 hours after the infusion.
key_findings.locator: Results > Additional Clinical and Adverse Events, and Safety Measures, 1st paragraph (p. 112, right column, continuing on p. 113); Results > Other Symptoms, last sentence (p. 112)
key_findings.note: No blood-pressure or pulse values are printed anywhere in the paper, so the cardiovascular statement cannot be quantified from it. The 48-hour assessment was an abbreviated unblinded rating with the BPRS and the adverse-events checklist and no cognitive testing (p. 108).

key_findings.finding: Speech and language: SANS alogia subscale scores rose between placebo and the moderate dose (t14=-1.74, p=0.05) and the high dose (t14=-2.07, p=0.03) and between the low and high doses (t14=-1.74, p=0.05), although the overall effect of condition was only a trend (F3,42=2.51, p=0.07, against a Bonferroni critical p of 0.01). The BPRS anxiety-depression subscale also changed (F3,42=5.73, p=0.002, critical p 0.0125), accounted for by increases in somatic concern. The authors state that formal thought disorder and language disorganization were not detected during the steady-state conditions apart from the alogia effect, but were noted during the loading doses.
key_findings.locator: Results > Other Symptoms, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 114, right column, continuing on p. 115)
key_findings.note: The pairwise comparisons are reported despite an overall test that does not meet the authors' own adjusted threshold; the observation about the loading doses is qualitative and unblinded.

reporting_issues.issue: Every paired post-hoc p value in the paper corresponds to a one-tailed test, which is nowhere stated. Editors' calculation: t14=2.17 printed as p=0.02 is p=0.048 two-tailed; t14=-1.95 printed as p=0.04 is p=0.07; t14=2.47 printed as p=0.01 is p=0.027; t13=3.30 printed as p=0.003 is p=0.006; t5=2.04 printed as p=0.05 is p=0.10; t7=2.78 printed as p=0.01 is p=0.027.
reporting_issues.consequence: Several comparisons that read as significant at p<0.05 are not significant on a two-tailed test, in particular the placebo against high dose comparison for BPRS negative symptoms and the first of the two delayed match to sample comparisons. Claims should cite the F tests for the effect of treatment condition and treat the individual dose-to-dose comparisons as one-tailed.

reporting_issues.issue: The infusion conditions are named throughout by their target steady concentrations (150, 45 and 13.5 ng/mL), but the measured concentrations plotted in Figure 6 are about 87 to 88 ng/mL and about 16 to 18 ng/mL, and the low condition never rose above the assay threshold. The paper does not state the measured steady values numerically and does not remark on the difference from target.
reporting_issues.consequence: A claim must not quote 150 or 45 ng/mL as concentrations achieved in this study. The encyclopedia should cite the measured values read from Figure 6, as approximations, and say that the lowest condition was below the limit of the assay.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract reports the BPRS negative symptom effect (F3,42=2.89, p=0.047) as one of the study's dose-dependent findings, but the Discussion's list of effects that survive Bonferroni adjustment (critical p 0.025 for the symptom measures) gives BPRS positive symptoms, SANS negative symptoms and verbal declarative memory, silently dropping the BPRS negative subscale.
reporting_issues.consequence: The negative-symptom finding is the weakest of the four headline results; a claim about ketamine-induced negative symptoms in healthy volunteers should rest on the SANS total rather than on the BPRS negative subscale, and should carry the p value as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: No table of cognitive means is given: the paragraph recall and delayed match to sample results appear only as plotted means with standard errors in Figures 4 and 5, and the four tasks with no detected effect (Stroop, continuous performance, verbal fluency, spatial delayed response) are reported without any statistics at all.
reporting_issues.consequence: The magnitude of the memory effects can be taken only from the one percentage the paper states (an 18.6% fall in total paragraph recall from placebo to the high dose) or read approximately from the figures, and the null results cannot be quantified or re-analysed; they should be reported as 'no effect was detected', never as evidence that these functions are unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: The delayed match to sample effect is significant in the univariate analysis and not significant in the multivariate analysis, and the paper reports the univariate result in the abstract and figures while mentioning the discrepancy only in the text; the post-hoc tests for that task carry 5 and 7 degrees of freedom, implying 6 to 8 complete pairs, and the number of participants contributing is never stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: The non-verbal memory finding should be cited only as preliminary, as the authors themselves label it, and never as an equal companion to the paragraph-recall result.

reporting_issues.issue: Plasma norketamine rose steadily throughout both measurable conditions and did not reach a steady state (in the high condition from 37.5 ng/mL at 20 minutes to 79.5 at 120), so the study's steady-state claim holds for ketamine only; the contribution of norketamine is dismissed on the basis of unpublished data from two of the authors.
reporting_issues.consequence: The exposure during the assessments was a steady ketamine concentration together with a rising norketamine concentration; a claim tying effects to a concentration should say which compound was held steady, and the norketamine potency statement cannot be verified.

reporting_issues.issue: The number of participants contributing to each analysis is never stated and has to be inferred from degrees of freedom, which vary between F3,42 (15 participants), F3,41, F3,40 and post-hoc tests on 13, 14, 7 and 5 degrees of freedom. Missing data are attributed to technical problems and to one participant who could not complete the battery because of nausea at the high dose, which is a drug effect.
reporting_issues.consequence: The effective sample size of each cognitive result is uncertain, and missing data at the high dose are not missing at random, so the high-dose means may be slightly favourable; both should be stated when the results are cited.

reporting_issues.issue: Blood pressure, pulse and oxygen saturation were monitored at 0, 20, 60 and 120 minutes, but no values, test statistics or p values for them are printed; the cardiovascular results are given in one qualitative sentence.
reporting_issues.consequence: This study cannot be cited for the size of ketamine's cardiovascular effects, only for the statement that they were transient in these conditions.

reporting_issues.issue: The study used the original, wider description of the BPRS hallucinatory behavior item so that perceptual distortions as well as hallucinations could be scored on it, and this item is one of the three in the positive symptom subscale.
reporting_issues.consequence: The BPRS positive subscale scores in this study are not comparable with studies that score that item in the usual way, and the rise cannot be read as evidence of hallucinations; the paper's own examples are perceptual distortions.

reporting_issues.issue: The intervals between the four infusion days are given only as non-consecutive days with a mean of 2.6 days (SD 1.1), and no period or order effect is reported; nor is it stated how many participants received each condition first.
reporting_issues.consequence: Carryover is implausible at these intervals, but a period effect on the repeated cognitive battery cannot be ruled out from the report; the counterbalanced task sets make a systematic practice bias unlikely.
